Pele Yoetz 140:1: Suspect - They said, of blessed memory (Derech Eretz Rabbah, ch. 5): let all people be suspect in your eyes as robbers, in order to guard against them. And if this was said in order to guard one's body and money, all the more so regarding prohibitions - one must suspect every person lest he not be as careful as is proper, and should not rely on anyone regarding foods and drinks until the matter is clear to him that the person is as careful as he himself is - and especially if he is already suspect, such that he cannot be trusted even under oath, for one suspected of a matter neither judges it nor testifies about it. And happy is the man who does this, that he not go to eat in another's house, for not everyone is careful about guarding wines from contact with a gentile, and they are not careful about checking for worms found in leavened grain and in vegetables, and about washing hands in the morning as is proper, and about cleanliness from milk and from meat with milk, and about keeping the Sabbath by not heating water through a gentile, and the like.
Pele Yoetz 140:2: But not everyone can do this, for some are considered arrogant for it, and if he does not go to their celebration there is a matter of enmity and spoiling the feast - and moreover, if he wishes to do this and act with such piety, the complete ones did not practice it, and many gossip about him afterward, saying he casts aspersions on the earlier ones, saying, "did we not see sages and pious men [eat there]?" Therefore, not everyone who wishes to take the Name and practice this piety can do it - only men who are not so much in the category of importance and about whom people do not care so much whether they go or not, they can be more careful not to go to just anyone's home.
Pele Yoetz 140:3: And whoever is compelled to go, in any case let him make a small rescue by asking them if they were careful to check for worms and not to heat water on the Sabbath. And if he cannot do this, at least let him withdraw his hand from the food as much as he can in a manner that they not notice, and He, being merciful, shall atone, for great is a transgression for its own sake (Horayot 10b). And in any case, if he can find a pretext to make a general fence, a general prohibition against eating any meal outside his own home, happy is he, for it is a great fence for his soul, for many evils follow from eating outside one's home in the company of people, and the time of eating is a time of war, a time of danger. Therefore how good and how pleasant is the portion of men who do not go out to feast outside their homes - especially at an optional feast, absence is good and presence is evil. In any case, on the festival of Passover, every person can be careful not to feast outside his own home, and there is no arrogance or exactingness in this, for it is already a common saying among people, "on Passover, a man does not eat at his brothers'" - for not everyone is equal in their carefulness, and whoever increases in carefulness is praiseworthy.
Pele Yoetz 141:1: Groom - Our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 6b): whoever benefits from a groom's feast and does not gladden him transgresses with five voices, and if he gladdens him he merits the Torah, which was given with five voices. And every person is obligated only according to his own measure, to do whatever is in his power to gladden the groom, doing what seems to him to be his wish - such as singing before him and speaking jesting words before him, and the like, matters that involve no neglect of fear of the Creator. But such a thing should not be found in Israel, to sing melodies of gentiles or melodies of lust, and to speak vulgar and mocking words in order to gladden the groom - what benefit is there if he gladdens the groom's heart while his own soul mourns over him for angering his Creator?
Pele Yoetz 141:2: And the essence of the groom's joy shall be when he is informed of what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, have revealed to us, that whoever marries a wife has all his sins forgiven (Yerushalmi Bikkurim 3:3; see Rashi, Genesis 29:9[?]) - therefore it is a time to have mercy on his own soul, that he be careful and guard against returning again to folly. And let one say to him: see your own affection before the Omnipresent, who forgives you all your sins, and He has said that you are comparable to a king, whom all are obligated to honor, and He desires your joy and has greatly commanded us to gladden you. Rejoice, young man, for this is the day the LORD has made, that you rejoice in it, and this day goes and shall not return, comparable to a wedding celebration - it is impossible not to rejoice with the joy of a mitzvah over the great goodness the LORD has done for you, that He has brought you to this time and created for you gladness and joy - and He Himself gladdens the groom with the bride, and these matters are ancient, and would that we knew what your wish is and with what to gladden you! Such and similar things, whatever is in one's power to do, let it be done to gladden the groom. And the women shall gladden the bride.
Pele Yoetz 141:3: And we find that great men of the world (Ketubot 17a) would dance before the bride, since they had no evil inclination - but now, permission has not been given for men and women to mingle even at a time of death, God forbid, all the more so at a time of gladness, for if there is mingling of men and women, Satan dances among them and brings forth the sword, and joy is turned to sorrow, God forbid. Rather, the groom sits among the men and the bride among the women, so that these not see those. And they said (Yalkut Shimoni, II Kings, remez 232) about Jezebel that when the dogs devoured her, they did not touch her head, her hands, and her feet, because she would go out to meet a bride and dance and clap before her. Therefore let every person lower his own honor a bit for the honor of Heaven, and gladden the groom and bride, and through this he shall rejoice in his own works and sit at the wedding.
Pele Yoetz 141:4: And it is the custom of Israel, Torah, to make "grooms of the Torah" [Chatan Torah] during Simchat Torah, and it is a time of joy for all Israel - let Israel rejoice in its Maker with the joy of a mitzvah for the completion of the Torah. And likewise increasing joy, especially at the time of the seven hakafot, is the custom of pious men and men of deeds, to leap and dance before the Torah scrolls with songs and praises and gladness and joy, and it is a wondrous means to merit for himself and his offspring the crown of Torah. And it is the custom of the "grooms" to increase somewhat in the feast and to gladden their circle of companions with the joy of a mitzvah, and certainly it is a great mitzvah, and the leaders of the communities must institute regulations to minimize expenses so that it not be too burdensome and every person can do it, for it is fitting for every person to do this too, once in his life. But these are matters that have no fixed measure - that there not be a mitzvah performed through a transgression, and where there is rejoicing there should be trembling, and God forbid that the offspring of Israel should transgress the Torah on the day of Simchat Torah - rather, let Israel rejoice in its Maker according to the Torah, in measure and in proportion, and through this they shall merit the crown of Torah, and to see the building of the chosen House, which shall be built speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 142:1: Debt - It is a good trait in a person that when he has a debt, he shall not rest nor be at ease until he repays his debts - this brings good to himself, for people say that whoever is a good payer is master of others' purses, for he acquires a good name for himself and finds it easy to borrow and take on credit whenever he wishes, as much as he wishes, and can become rich, for a person profits more through the trustworthiness with which people trust him than he profits through his own money. Therefore, whoever is a good merchant, this shall be the beginning of his own kingdom: that he acquire trustworthiness by repaying a debt in its proper time, and if he does not have it, let him borrow from another for a time in order to repay this one, and afterward borrow from this one to repay the other - so shall he do repeatedly, taking the cap from one and placing it on the other, in a manner that he renews the old loan and does not lose his trustworthiness. And he performs a mitzvah too, for they said (Ketubot 86a): repayment of a debt is a mitzvah. And he performs an act of kindness by not locking the door before borrowers. And whoever is careful in this and has this trait - when he has a debt, he shall not rest until he repays it - let him reason a fortiori regarding himself: all the more so must he be alert to repay a debt he has with the Omnipresent, and be among the alert who hasten to mitzvot, and a mitzvah that comes to his hand, let him not let it turn sour, and he shall not rest nor be at ease until he performs it.
Pele Yoetz 142:2: And on the other hand, the creditor of his fellow is under the mitzvah not to press his fellow and his brother if he knows he has nothing, and even to pass before him is forbidden. And even if he suspects him of being a cheat who has money but shows that he has none, he must still be concerned lest the truth be as claimed, and shall be in awe of transgressing "you shall not press" (Exodus 22:24), until the matter is clear to him that he has money or something of monetary value, real estate or movable property, with which he could repay his debt - then he is not obligated to have mercy on him, for this one shall not enjoy another's money and rejoice, but rather let him compel him by all manner of coercion, through the courts of Israel and by permission of the court, or, in a place where there is no court, let him compel him through the courts of gentiles, that his soul be pressed and he repay his debt even from the cloak on his shoulder. But in any case, even here one must conduct himself in the way of the good and the straight path, which is honor to the one who does it and honor to him from mankind, and he should not stand on strict Torah law but act beyond the letter of the law. And if he suspects him of being a cheat and acting improperly, unwilling to repay his debt, then he too may act improperly with him and collect from him whatever he can, even the cloak from his shoulder.
Pele Yoetz 142:3: And if he is a good man walking in innocence, economizing and wishing to repay, gradually accumulating payment as much as he can, coin by coin, then it is good and upright in the eyes of God and man that he not press him to take from him his house and household items, and not cause him to stumble by publicizing that he is a creditor of his and taking from him goods and merchandise for his debt through litigation, for this cuts off his legs, destroying his trustworthiness, and his evil is great. Therefore let him do this to fulfill his obligation to Heaven and to people: that he give him time and collect from him even coin by coin, for every coin joins to the reckoning. And if he can, let him lend him a hand so that he can earn and be able to repay, and also eat bread - and this is a great mitzvah, fulfilling what the Torah said (Leviticus 25:35), "if your brother becomes poor and his hand falters, you shall strengthen him," and this is the greatest of charities. And with the measure a person measures, it is measured to him (Megillah 12b) - for every person is a creditor entitled to collect his debt immediately, without delay. But in any case, just as a person does not forgive his own debt, so the Holy One, blessed be He, is not lenient but rather is patient and collects His own [debt] eventually.
Pele Yoetz 142:4: Therefore let the living take to heart to do whatever is in his power to do to repay his debt little by little, as much as he can, before the collectors come who return repeatedly and collect from a person with or without his knowledge - and this is the trait of the righteous court, that when a person pays of his own good will, the little adds up to a great reckoning (as in the law of a bailee (Bava Metzia 34a), that if he paid and did not wish to swear because he did not want to trouble the court, they grant him double payment and payment of four and five) (as I shall write under the entry "Yisurin" [sufferings]).
Pele Yoetz 142:5: And behold, I, in my poverty, could exempt the entire world from judgment based on the principle we hold: "he says it is permitted, he is coerced" (Makkot 7b) - and since the way of a man is straight in his own eyes, it turns out that he says it is permitted and he is coerced, for it is rare that he knows his Master and intends to rebel against Him. But this argument benefits only one who judges everyone favorably by this argument and is not exacting about anything and overlooks his own traits [being wronged] - then they overlook all his own transgressions, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Megillah, ibid.): with the measure a person measures, it is measured to him. If he judges unfavorably, he is judged unfavorably, and whoever judges favorably, the Omnipresent judges him favorably.
Pele Yoetz 143:1: Lack - There is no person without some lack in traits and in knowledge, and every man is a liar - just as it is impossible to have grain without straw and there is no wood without smoke, so there is no person without error, and there is none complete in the world except the Rock, whose work is perfect, for all His ways are justice (Deuteronomy 32:4). Therefore one should not blame a person in whom is found something not good, for he too, like him, has lacks found in him - rather, "a person sees all blemishes except his own blemishes" (Nega'im 2:5), and a person does not see fault in himself, and it is possible that his own lack exceeds his fellow's, according to what kind of person he is. And an obligation rests upon every person to contemplate, understand, and comprehend what he lacks, and if he does not understand it in his own mind, let him listen to counsel and go to the wise and become wise, or ask everyone whether there is someone who knows something to tell him - and he should not be angry if they tell him of some lack he has, as is the custom of some boors, and should not seek to maintain his own position with false and rejected arguments, for this is the way of the wicked - rather, let a person be God-fearing and acknowledge the truth even if it does not fit his own mind and his way is straight in his eyes; let him accept the truth from whoever is greater than him in wisdom and in number, and nullify his own opinion before theirs, and change his ways, his conduct, and his deeds from day to day until he acquires as much perfection as he can - for they said (Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 25): a person is obligated to say, "when shall my deeds reach the deeds of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob?"
Pele Yoetz 143:2: And so one must hold gratitude and much favor and kindness toward whoever informs him of his own lack, and of this it is said (Proverbs 19:8[?] - actually 9:8), "rebuke a wise man and he shall love you" - for there is no favor greater than this, for just as they said (Bamidbar Rabbah 21:4) that whoever causes another to sin does him more harm than one who kills him, correspondingly, whoever brings merit to his fellow does him more good than if he had revived him after death. And even if, in truth, he has no lack and his fellow errs in his own imagination, in any case it is fitting to hold gratitude toward him for having thought to do him good - only he should not tell him in front of others if there is concern it will shame him and make his reputation foul, for then the favor is weighed and thrown to the dogs (Shabbat 63b). And in truth, there is no lack in the world like a lack of knowledge, and there is no poverty like poverty of knowledge, as they said (Vayikra Rabbah 1:6): if you lack knowledge, what have you acquired? And this is the evil of man on earth, what King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 21:2): "the way of a man is straight in his own eyes." And he said (ibid. 26:12): "you have seen a man wise in his own eyes - there is more hope for a fool than for him." Behold, therefore, the man who desires life shall not lean on his own understanding and shall nullify his own opinion and will before the opinion and will of others who teach him for his own benefit, and should not be content with his own lacks, saying, "my situation is that I am not like others who are lacking much more than I" - for this is great folly. Have you ever in your life seen a man to whom they offered a thousand gold pieces to keep, and he said, "I want only ten, for my situation is that I am not like others who have only five"? Or would a man say, "I wish, of my own soul's desire, to receive ten lashes, for my situation is that I am not like others who receive a hundred or a thousand lashes"? Certainly, if such a man were found, he would be called a fool and a madman - so it is with this matter.
Pele Yoetz 143:3: And behold, it is a correct and true thing to look at those beneath oneself regarding the affairs and possessions of this world, for for every kind of evil and lack there is someone worse off, and this shall be his comfort, and he shall rejoice in his own portion, his allotted lot. And all the more so since all evils and lacks began with the great men of the world. Adam, the first man, had his son killed by his own brother. Abraham our father and Isaac our father had Ishmael and Esau come forth from them. Jacob our father encountered many evils - pursued by Esau and Laban, his daughter was defiled, his wife died, and his son was lost to him for twenty-two years. Moses our teacher fled from before Pharaoh and sat imprisoned in Jethro's house for ten years (as stated in Sefer HaYashar). And likewise Joseph the righteous was afflicted with an iron fetter on his foot; his soul came into iron for twelve years. Aaron the priest had his two sons, great young men of the world, die in one day. Saul the king was killed along with three of his sons in one day. King David encountered many evils - pursued by Saul, fled from his son Absalom, and Absalom and his son Amnon were killed. King Solomon was restless and wandering in the land, wandering for bread (Gittin 68b). And many such evils befell the righteous, the arms and foundations of every generation, and especially you have given them the cup of poverty and the pail of destitution to drink - many, such as Hillel (Yoma 35b), Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat (Ta'anit 25a), Rabbi Yehuda bar Ila'i (Sanhedrin 20a), and many like them, complete men, and likewise many are found in every generation who suffer poverty and harsh sufferings of various kinds - this shall be the comfort of the man whom the LORD desires to crush with some suffering and lack: let him sit alone and be silent and accept the judgment of Heaven with joy, believing with complete faith that whatever the Merciful One does, He does for good (Berachot 60b), for his own benefit and his own good, as is fitting for a merciful Father, the Master of mercy. And let him say: the Rock, whose work is perfect, for all His ways are justice (Deuteronomy 32:4), for I am no better than these complete men, and there is already no complete good in this world, and there is no person without some evil and some lack - and one must accept it with joy and give thanks to the LORD and bless over the evil as over the good, and say, "bless the LORD, O my soul," and so on, "for He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor requited us according to our iniquities" (Psalms 103:10).
Pele Yoetz 143:4: And if the LORD has bestowed good upon him, let him always fear lest he consume his own world in his lifetime, and let him always say, "I am unworthy of all the kindnesses," and in order not to deduct from his own merits and also so that his possessions endure, let him do as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ketubot 66b[?]): the salt of money is diminishing [i.e., giving charity]. And let him increase performing kindness with his own good fortune, with which the LORD has graced him - with his body, his money, the houses he has, and his wisdom, and the like - and through this, "the righteous shall be repaid on earth," and his reward shall be complete.
Pele Yoetz 144:1: Regret - The essence of repentance is complete regret, that one regret what he did improperly, like one who regrets having killed his own only son in his anger or his drunkenness, and if he can revive him, let him do whatever is in his power to do. And it is true that even the wicked are full of regrets - as soon as he does something improper and the evil inclination has left him, he immediately regrets a little and says, "would that I had not done it - it would have been better" - as though even now it is good, but it would have been better had he not done it. And this is because the evil inclination minimizes the transgression and diminishes it in his eyes, as the commentators explained on the verse (Genesis 6:5), "and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil" - "only" is a limiting term - and this too happens when there remains a moist trace of vitality, that he has not sunk so deeply into that transgression, but if habit has made it to him as though permitted, his heart shall not grieve over it, for it is in his heart to wonder when it will come to his hand again and he shall do it.
Pele Yoetz 144:2: But the man whose heart the fear of the LORD has touched, his own soul lives if, when his inclination overpowers him and he transgresses a transgression, then, when his eyes are opened in his old age and he remembers what he did in his youth, his heart shall tremble within him with anguish like a woman in labor, and it shall be bitter to him, and streams of water shall flow from his eyes more than one whose dead lies before him - for so is it fitting and proper for whoever has defied the word of his Master, an exalted and lofty Master, and has angered Him to His face. And our teacher Yonah has already written in Sha'arei Teshuvah that according to the grief and sighing with which one sighs, with a broken back, over the iniquity, so shall the man be cleansed of iniquity - and these are sufferings of love that come according to the greatness of love one has with the Creator, more than for his own only son, his own spirit, and his own soul, and therefore his own spirit is grieved over how he did such a great evil, and this shall be his life and his great deliverance, for through this he shall repair his own perversion and make a fence so as not to add to his sin. And the great fence is to think thoughts before doing anything at all, even a matter of mitzvah, for "the fruit of haste is regret" (Mivchar HaPeninim 43:27). And deliberateness, deliberateness, assures him that he shall not sin, and no mishap or unfixed matter shall be found with him - rather, he does everything well in its proper time, for he shall see with his own eyes and his heart shall understand the end of a matter from its beginning, and he shall find the means of his own redemption.
Pele Yoetz 145:1: Chol HaMoed [Intermediate Festival Days] - Well known is the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory (Sanhedrin 99a), that whoever disgraces the appointed times, that is, Chol HaMoed, has no portion in the World to Come. And they explained that this refers to one who conducts himself as on a weekday regarding work, or eating and drinking. And let the man tremble and be seized, for there are things that appear light and a person tramples them underfoot, about which they said that whoever transgresses them has no portion in the World to Come - and especially regarding Chol HaMoed, many have transgressed, and because certain kinds of work were permitted more than on a festival day, all kinds of work have become as permitted, and no one seeks to know what is forbidden and what is permitted, and one transgression drags another, for since they are obsessed with their business or with playing cards, the day passes without eating at all, or with only minimal eating, as on a weekday, and may the good LORD atone for this. And the man who fears for his own soul shall inquire from a book or from teachers which work is forbidden and which is permitted, and shall not transgress. And likewise let him be careful to increase somewhat in eating and drinking to distinguish between the holy and the mundane, and not destroy himself knowingly.
Pele Yoetz 145:2: And well known is their saying, of blessed memory (Yerushalmi Shabbat 15:3), that Sabbaths and festivals were given to Israel only for engagement in Torah. And well known is what the early sages explained on the verse (Psalms 75:3), "when I take the appointed time, I shall judge with equity" - for those who have an excuse that they cannot engage in Torah due to their preoccupation with earning a livelihood and sustenance, Chol HaMoed is their blessing, and it cuts off their legs [excuse], for its very existence provides also for the time of their preoccupation, for Chol HaMoed comes to hasten so that preoccupation not be a cause [for neglect]. And if, on Chol HaMoed, and likewise at every time he is free, he does not free himself for idleness but rather engages in Torah, he comes with his reward also for the time he is preoccupied with his business, as though he were engaged in Torah. And the man who fears the LORD shall be clothed in dread all his days and shall be careful of the affront to the Torah, for whoever does not engage in Torah is called rebuked (Shemot Rabbah 41:9). And all the more so shall he tremble and fear on Chol HaMoed, for these are days of judgment - for on Passover the world is judged regarding grain, and on the festival [of Sukkot] regarding water (Rosh Hashanah 16a), and the conclusion of judgment is on Hoshana Rabbah, and the record book is open to judge him according to his deeds, and it is fitting to gird strength to add one more mitzvah - and this suffices for whoever has a heart.
Pele Yoetz 146:1: The Destruction of the Temple - The destruction of the Temple must be a remembrance between our eyes, as it is written (Psalms 137:5), "if I forget you, O Jerusalem," and so on. And especially at mealtime, let it be remembered, and his soul shall be bowed down over it, that his own table is full of abundance while our Father in Heaven's table has been empty for these several hundred years because of our many sins. And likewise at night, at the beginning of the watches, let him recite the order of Tikkun Chatzot with a voice of weeping, mourning, and lament, more than one whose dead lies before him - for so is it fitting for whoever has a heart and eyes to see, except that because of our many transgressions our eyes have grown dim from seeing the evil we have caused above. And let every person do whatever is in his power to do, as I have written under the entry "Mourning for the Destruction of the Temple" - see there.
Pele Yoetz 146:2: And how many things our Rabbis, of blessed memory, forbade because of the destruction of the Temple - such as what they said (Berachot 31a): it is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world. And they also said (Gittin 7a): singing is forbidden, as it is written (Hosea 9:1), "do not rejoice, O Israel, with exultation like the peoples." And they further said in the Talmud (Sotah 48a): the ear that hears singing shall be uprooted. And they said (ibid.): singing in a house is destruction on the threshold. And it is fitting for the great men of every generation, in every single city, to make a fence and forbid it as a prohibition, and especially regarding gentile songs, where there is an additional prohibition, since they contain much vulgarity and mockery - let a man muster his strength to nullify this bad custom, for they said in the Talmud (ibid.) that Rav Huna abolished singing, and a hundred geese sold for a zuz and a hundred se'ah of wheat sold for a zuz, yet they were not desired [there was no demand, showing prosperity]. Rav Chisda came and treated it lightly [reinstating singing], and a goose was sought for a zuz and could not be found [scarcity resulted]. Go out and learn its severity, and how Heaven is exacting about this, and gird your loins like a man to keep the many from transgression, and speak to a hundred, and if not, to one - and in any case, it should not be beyond him to protest to the members of his own household and not let any gentile song be heard from their mouths, but rather at a time of gladness let them sing a song and praise to the Holy One, blessed be He, and through this Israel shall rejoice in its Maker and the LORD shall rejoice in His works. And it is especially necessary to be careful on the Sabbath, to remember at his meals the destruction of the Temple, since he says in the Grace after Meals, "and although we have eaten and drunk, we have not forgotten the destruction of Your great and holy House" - and if he does not remember and the destruction of the Temple does not come to his heart even at the time he says these words, he testifies falsely about himself before his Maker and bears his own iniquity. But whoever brings up Jerusalem in his remembrance shall merit to see its rebuilding.
Pele Yoetz 147:1: Favor - "Grace and honor the LORD shall give" (Psalms 84:12), for there is a thing that two men do or say equally, and one finds favor while the other is burdensome as a heavy load. And of this we pray every day, "and grant us favor, kindness, and mercy in Your eyes and in the eyes of all who see us." And understanding is needed to comprehend and get to the bottom of people's minds, so as not to do or say except what one knows for certain, without any doubt, will find favor, and will be pleasant to all the listeners, not merely to some of them. And whenever his heart hesitates and is concerned that it might not find favor, he shall refrain, for absence is good.
Pele Yoetz 147:2: And it is true that one must find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man, but the essence is to find favor in the eyes of the LORD, not to anger the LORD, heaven forbid, in order to find favor in the eyes of man, as is the custom of certain boors who increase jest and frivolity and mocking and vulgar speech before certain rich (bad) men in order to increase the laughter and find favor in their eyes so that they grant them a handout - and some do this even without any benefit at all, simply to gladden people, for this is what a person's own inclination does: when he says something and the listeners are gladdened and laugh at his words, his heart is widened and he rejoices and is glad at having achieved such a merit that they laugh at his words, and he thinks of what other bad things he might say, similar to these, so that they continue to laugh and be gladdened. Woe to the speakers and alas for those who laugh - both of these shall be burned in the house of ashes. And whoever has a little brain in his skull shall see that this is a foolish way, for what does it give him and what does it add for him to act crazily and increase transgressions in order for others to laugh? And if they think to find favor and profit, do they not know that they lose more than they profit, and such a spirit shall benefit them only for evil, besides their punishment reserved for them in the World to Come? Therefore let every clever person act with knowledge, and if he can act in a manner that finds favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man, how good and how pleasant! And if he must nullify the will of the Creator in order to find favor in the eyes of man, God forbid that he do this - it is better that he be hated and abhorred in the eyes of all people and find favor before the God of the universe, and a good man manages his affairs with judgment.
Pele Yoetz 148:1: Deaf - There are several things regarding which it is fitting to be as one deaf, not to hear, and to make oneself as one who does not know - such as, if people (who are violent men and licentious ones of the generation, whom Heaven has favored to be treated with honor) once or twice stepped out of line and opposed him behind his back and spoke disparagingly of him, with insults and curses, let his own spirit be guarded not to let it be known that he knows all this - for then the licentious ones shall say, "since we have become foul in his eyes, from now on we shall anger him to his face as well" - but if they do not know that he knows, perhaps they shall regret what they did and treat him with honor, at least to his face. And likewise, if they spoke some secret matter and it happened that he knew and heard, let him make himself as one deaf who did not hear, so that they not be distressed by his having heard, and it not be heard from his own mouth. And likewise let him hold his own mouth shut at a time of quarrel and make himself as one deaf who does not hear, and shall not answer whether for good or for evil, and through this he gives his own cheek to the one who strikes him, and shall be filled with disgrace (Lamentations 3:30), and in the end the one who strikes him for this shall also be as one mute who does not open his mouth. And even a father with his sons, and a teacher with his students, and a husband with his wife, and a master with his servants, and the like - it is fitting not to be so exacting with them, and sometimes to make himself as one who did not see and did not hear and did not know. And likewise, if a man heard something improper about his fellow, let him make himself as one deaf who did not hear and as though he did not know, so that his fellow not be ashamed before him because of it. And in all such cases, let the wise man hear and add learning: there are times when one must make known and let it be heard that he hears and knows, and there are times when one must be as a man who does not hear.
Pele Yoetz 149:1: Letter Tet: Impurity - It is fitting for a person to be careful of all impurity, for impurity dulls the heart, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yoma 39a) on the verse (Leviticus 11:43), "and you shall become impure through them" - meaning, that his heart becomes dulled, closed, sealed, and stopped from being able to do good, because of our many sins, and because of "you have defiled the land" of the nations and the like. At the very least, is it not good to choose the lesser evil and be careful about what is in our power to be careful of? And I have already written just above, under the entry "Purity," some things that defile, which one must be careful of and purify. However, there are further things one must be careful not to be defiled by - I shall mention a few of them that come to my memory now; let the wise man hear and add learning.
Pele Yoetz 149:2: It is written in the book "Brit Olam," which is glosses on Sefer Chasidim, siman 435: a certain Jew walked in the courtyard of a gentile temple; when he went out, he heard a heavenly voice saying, "you have cast Me behind your back," and he fasted all his days. And Rabbi Chesed L'Avraham wrote: whoever enters the courts of gentiles or their houses of worship and the like (such as gentile temples that contain idolatry) is under the wings of the Other Side, and they defile him little by little, and he does not know that it is at the cost of his own soul, and so on - see there. And if you value your own soul and take these words to heart, awaken and rouse yourself from the slumber of the evil inclination that spreads a net for your feet unknowingly, and from this you shall awaken and become alert to several matters that have become as permitted, and this suffices - to here are his words. And in the Holy Zohar, Parashat Vayechi, they said: a gentile who worships idols is impure, and whoever draws near him becomes impure. Behold, therefore, how good it is for whoever is among those who sit in the study house to be careful, as much as possible, not to touch an idol worshipper.
Pele Yoetz 149:3: And likewise one must be careful not to touch a carcass and any impure thing, and not to walk among the dead. And we have heard a warning from the disciples of the Ari, of blessed memory, not to go to the cemetery except for the burial of the dead, and therefore I refrain from going on Tisha B'Av and the like. And it is especially necessary to be careful and distance oneself from one's wife when she is a niddah, for they said in the Holy Zohar that there is no impurity in the world like the impurity of a niddah, which defiles from within and from without, both soul and body, and as soon as one draws near her, the impurity leaps upon him, as it is written (Leviticus 15:24), "and her
Pele Yoetz 149:4: menstrual impurity was upon him." And whatever son is born afterward, an unclean spirit rests upon him. And if they said this regarding his own wife, all the more so, a fortiori, regarding other men's wives - and more is written on this below under the entry "Niddah," with the help of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 149:5: And in the Holy Zohar, Parashat Tazria, they said: idolatrous gentiles build buildings for their own faces and their own defilement, and when they begin to build, they say a word, and since it is mentioned in their mouths, an unclean spirit rests upon it, and when the work is completed, the unclean spirit rests upon it. And therefore, whoever builds a building, when he begins to build, must mention in his mouth that he builds for the service of the Holy One, blessed be He, and then the assistance of the Holy One, blessed be He, rests upon him and holiness rests upon it, and of him it is said (Job 5:24), "and you shall know that your tent is at peace, and you shall visit your habitation and not sin." And one must mention this word with his mouth when he builds, and then "you shall not sin" - and if not, behold, the Other Side is ready to enter his house, and for as long as that building stands, it belongs to it, and a person can be harmed.
Pele Yoetz 149:6: Further there, Rabbi Elazar said: in all of a person's deeds, he must intend that they all be for the holy Name, mentioning with his mouth the holy Name over everything he does, that everything is for His service, and then the Other Side shall not rest upon him, because it is always ready to attach itself to a person and can rest upon that deed. This establishes the words of the Holy Zohar. Let the wise man hear, and let these words be as frontlets between his eyes and as a remembrance, that the Name of Heaven be fluent in his mouth regarding the building of houses, and making garments, and eating and drinking, and business, and all his deeds - let him say explicitly, with a full mouth, that he does it for the service of the blessed Name, and through this the defilements of the Other Side shall be purified and sanctified.
Pele Yoetz 149:7: And from what has been said, you shall hear that those who buy or rent houses, or take garments made by gentiles for themselves, or from men who are not proper and do not know how to be careful in this, do not do well. And even if it is cheap, compared to what he loses, according to the words of the Holy Zohar spoken truly, they stand at a great price - and let a man give all the wealth of his house for the love of the blessed Name, and better a little with intention than much without intention.
Pele Yoetz 150:1: Reason - It is good sense to know what the mitzvah is and what reason there is in it, and one should not perform a mitzvah learned by rote, for over this the Holy One, blessed be He, was angered, and said through Isaiah the prophet (29:13), "because this people draws near," and so on, "and their fear of Me is a commandment of men learned by rote - therefore behold, I shall again do a wondrous thing with this people, a wonder and a marvel," and so on, may the Merciful One save us. And sometimes a mitzvah without knowledge of its reason is like a body without a soul - such as the mitzvah of tzitzit, which our Former commanded us and revealed its reason, saying, "and you shall see it and remember all the mitzvot of the LORD," and so on, "in order that you remember," and so on (Numbers 15:39). And if he does not set his heart to remember, it turns out that he has not fulfilled the intention of our Former, and what benefit is there in his wearing tzitzit? And likewise in this manner regarding the wearing of tefillin and other mitzvot. Examine this and go deep into it, and you shall see how whoever does not know the reason for the mitzvot is almost bare of the mitzvot. And whoever does not have the heart to know shall ask, and shall roll in the dust of the feet of the sages in order to learn.
Pele Yoetz 150:2: And they have died [and I shall discuss] the benefit that follows from knowing the reasons for the mitzvot: that one comes to sanctify himself even in what is permitted to him - such as the prohibition of interest that the Torah forbade, and according to its reason, that the Holy One, blessed be He, wished that they perform kindness for free and gracious and kind loans, it is fitting to withdraw one's hand even from lending by way of a business partnership if possible for him, and likewise many such matters. And a further benefit of knowing the reasons for the mitzvot is that one can fulfill even the mitzvot that are not in his power to fulfill - such as the mitzvah of offering sacrifices, whose reason is so that he take it to heart that this is what would be fitting to be done to him, and his heart shall be humbled. Behold, therefore, even now he can fulfill "the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit" and all such things, for if a man sets his mind to it, let him hear and add learning. And regarding mitzvot that have no reason, let it be considered that the Holy One, blessed be He, wished to bring merit to Israel, therefore He multiplied for them Torah and mitzvot. And how good and how pleasant it is that before performing the mitzvah, he state with his mouth what this mitzvah is, and what reason there is in it, and how it is fitting to perform it - this is the straight path for whoever wishes to be a servant of God with complete service. And it is found in the Talmud (Yerushalmi Berachot 5:1[?]) that knowing the reason for a matter aids remembrance, but sometimes it is not good to reveal the reasons for laws to the ignorant, lest it cause them to break out, saying, "I shall increase and not be forbidden," or when that reason cannot enter their minds, and those erring in spirit shall not know that the words of the Torah and the words of the Sages live and endure forever and for all eternity.
Pele Yoetz 151:1: Preoccupation - Preoccupation is a thing that spoils all service, and the complete man must settle his mind and cast his burden upon the LORD, and when preoccupation of the heart comes to him, let him consider the love and fear of the LORD, and let him picture to himself a man who has business dealings to earn a thousand thousand gold denarii - if they call him elsewhere to earn a single penny, he shall raise his voice with a mighty voice and say, "leave me be, I am not free, I have much business, and I am not concerned about losing a penny, for I have no leisure to attend to it." And all the more so, if he bears the burden of the LORD's word, the blessed Name shall bear his burden, and "those who hope in the LORD shall renew their strength" (Isaiah 40:31). And they already told a parable on this in the Midrash (Shocher Tov, Psalms 17): one man sat in Tiberias and had a field in Sepphoris, and another from Sepphoris had a field in Tiberias, until they said to each other, "guard mine and I shall guard yours." So it is with the fear of Heaven on earth - everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven, and bread is from heaven. The Holy One, blessed be He, said, "guard Mine and I shall guard yours." And let a person observe his sons and the members of his household, how they do not trouble their minds over livelihood or anything at all, being dependent on their father, who is flesh and blood like them, and they say, "what is this trouble to us? Let our father live [and provide]" - we, who have to rely and lean upon our Father in Heaven, all the more so! Such and similar things let the living take to heart, and he shall live a life of contentment, and cling to his Maker and to the service of the blessed Name.
Pele Yoetz 152:1: Nature - An obligation rests upon every person to conduct himself according to nature in guarding his health and earning his livelihood, as I have written above under the entry "Da'at" [knowledge]. But our eyes see that many have done this and it did not help, even though they conducted themselves according to nature and greatly guarded their health and strove greatly to earn through every kind of diligence, and yet ended up with nothing. And from this a person must believe and remember what the Torah said (Deuteronomy 8:18), "and you shall remember that it is He who gives you strength to make wealth." And whatever happens to a person according to nature, whether good or bad, is all by the decree of the Most High God, according to a person's own deeds - except that if he steps out of line and causes evil to himself according to nature, granted the matter is decreed from Heaven, but nevertheless he is liable for his own soul and destined to give judgment for having acted improperly.
Pele Yoetz 152:2: And this is a deep inquiry that has no answer due to the limited grasp of man and the depth of the laws of the Creator of the world, for a person's heart shall strain, saying: if evils according to nature are also by the decree of the Most High, why then is he punished for stepping out of line in this and the like? They said (Chagigah 13a) regarding this and similar matters: do not inquire into what is beyond you. And regarding this the Tanna taught (Avot 3:15): everything is foreseen, yet permission is granted. And Maimonides, of blessed memory, explained that the Holy One, blessed be He, knows everything, but His knowledge does not compel, and a person can do what his heart desires, and therefore he is destined to give judgment for stepping out of line. And regarding this matter, a person must be strong in his faith, to believe with strong faith that this is indeed the truth, and that the Rock's work is perfect, He is righteous and upright, and that this matter is beyond him because His knowledge is not like our knowledge, and His ways are higher than our ways. And "the righteous shall live by his faith" (Habakkuk 2:4). And therefore, even if evil comes to him through the hand of evil men, and they are destined to give judgment because they are chosen by free will, nevertheless, why should a living man complain, a man about his own sins, which caused it to him? Proof of this matter is the exile in Egypt, as it is written (Genesis 15:13), "know for certain that your descendants shall be strangers," "and also the nation whom they shall serve I shall judge." And it is written (Isaiah 10:5), "woe, Assyria, rod of My anger" - yet it is written (II Samuel 16:10), "the LORD has said to him, curse." And it is written (Deuteronomy 22:8), "if the one who falls should fall from it" - and this is clear and well known.
Pele Yoetz 152:3: Also, when illness or loss comes upon a person by way of nature, let him believe with complete faith that his own sins caused it. And therefore our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 5a): if a person sees that suffering comes upon him, let him examine his own deeds. And I have already heard of a certain man of deeds, God-fearing and turning away from evil, one of the men of our own generation, whose way this was: whenever some loss happened to him in his business, or over any loss he suffered, he would immediately return home from the market and confess and weep, saying, "my own iniquities have turned these away." But now, because of our sins, no one takes this to heart, but rather they search to find the matter by way of nature - "this illness came to him for this cause and that cause," "this loss came to him for this cause and that cause" - and gives no thought at all to examining his own deeds and repenting. And also those who come to console him say this: "such is the way of the world, evils go about in the world, many have drunk of this," and the like, and no one tells him that rebukes come for iniquity. And it is likewise fitting in this time that if one were to tell him this, that his sins have prevailed, it would turn out that instead of comforting him, he distresses him further, and there is a matter of enmity involved.
Pele Yoetz 152:4: And it is true that they also used to console this way in earlier generations, and it is fitting to console this way regarding the death of a soul - if a person of his has died, God forbid - for then he certainly justifies the judgment upon himself and remembers his own sins. But if his fellow were also to tell him that his sins killed the soul, his own flesh would grieve over him, and his own soul would mourn greatly over him, and he could come to danger, God forbid, from excessive grief - therefore one must remove this somewhat from his mind and speak to him words that settle the heart. But regarding sufferings that come upon him in his body or his money, it is fitting to tell him that it is not by way of chance, but rather everything is decreed from Heaven, with rebukes for iniquity from this transmigration or from previous transmigrations. And so we find regarding the early pious men, as brought in the Talmud (Berachot 5b), that Rav Huna's four hundred barrels of wine turned sour, and the Rabbis went in to him and said to him, "let the master examine his own conduct," for the Holy One, blessed be He, is not suspected of executing judgment without justice. And in these orphaned generations, such as we, orphans of orphans, there is no need to examine, for from head to foot there is nothing sound in us - rather, this is the way of the upright man: when any evil at all comes to him, whether in his body, his money, or his honor, he is immediately obligated to show in himself that he feels it is not by way of chance, and through this the servant shall be reconciled to his Master, that the servant shall immediately say this or a similar formula according to the eloquence of his own tongue, even in the vernacular:
Pele Yoetz 152:5: Master of the universe, I know my own disgrace and my shame and my humiliation, for I have greatly angered You, and in justice You have chastised me in my body (or he may say: in my money, or: in my honor). Please, LORD our God and God of our fathers, may our prayer come before You, and so on, until "and You are righteous regarding all that has come upon us, for You have acted in truth," and so on. And Yours, O LORD, is kindness, for You repay each man according to his deeds, to atone for our sins and to guide us in Your service. And so, please, O God, merciful Father, as a father has mercy on his children, have mercy on us. Help us, God of our salvation, for the sake of the honor of Your Name, and save us and atone for our sins for the sake of Your Name. And set us right, our King, with good counsel from before You, so that we may walk in the way of the good and keep the paths of the righteous. And may the words of my mouth and the meditation of my heart be acceptable before You, O LORD, my Rock and my Redeemer.
